papers.version_note: arXiv:1512.02900v1 [quant-ph], 9 Dec 2015, dated December 10, 2015 in the title block; the text layer holds one copy of the paper. Pages are counted from the 38 page breaks of the text layer; the printed page numbers are used in anchors. Several equations and the table in Appendix C came through the text layer garbled (symbols lost, columns split); claims that rest only on such material are not quoted.
papers.what_it_is: A review written by first-year students of the Bristol Quantum Engineering Centre for Doctoral Training that surveys quantum machine learning algorithms and experiments up to 2015, lists challenges (state preparation, readout, QRAM), and adds an appendix proposing a 'weights in states' quantum perceptron trained with the HHL algorithm.

it is currently unclear whether this will be possible.

this document summarises the output of the ‘Cohort Project’ postgraduate unit.

assertions.value: The authors state that the field's outlook is generally positive, showing significant promise; that they have found no reason why learning algorithms cannot be run on a quantum machine, but that there are appreciable hurdles before it can be claimed to be a primary application of quantum computation; and that current focus should be on algorithms that show an appreciation of the practical difficulties of implementation.
quotes: The ﬁeld’s outlook is generally positive, showing signiﬁcant promise
We have found no reason as to why this cannot occur, however there are appreciable hurdles to overcome before one can claim that it is a primary application of quantum computation.
We believe current focus should be on the development of quantum machine learning algorithms that show an appreciation of the practical diﬃculties of implementation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own overall judgment of a literature review; not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that significant real-world applications demonstrate an obvious market for implementing learning algorithms on a quantum machine.

assertions.reader_inference: The introduction cites only a data mining textbook (reference 1) for the breadth of applications and market; the paper gives no market data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first problem encountered with quantum machine learning is its definition, and that the grouping of scenarios into categories is subjective, so any deep theoretical meaning requires further clarification.
quotes: The ﬁrst problem encountered with quantum machine learning (QML) is its deﬁnition.
This is subjective and any deep theoretical meaning requires further clariﬁcation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the status of their own categorisation.

assertions.value: The authors define three learning categories, loosely based on Aimeur, Brassard and Gambs: L0 is classical machine learning on a classical machine, including machine learning on a classical machine with data that came from a quantum system; L1, denoted QML, runs the learning process predominantly with classical computation with only part of the protocol, such as a sub-routine, requiring access to a quantum computer; L2, also considered QML, has no sub-routine that can be performed equally well on a classical computer.
quotes: First, we consider the classical case, which deﬁnes the category L0.
Also included is machine learning performed on a classical machine but with data that has come from a quantum system
The second category, L1, we will denote as QML.
Here, the learning process can predominantly be run with classical computation, with only part of the protocol (e.g. a particular sub-routine) requiring access to a quantum computer.
We will denote the ﬁnal learning category as L2; this is also considered to be QML.
Here, the algorithm contains no sub-routine that can be performed equally well on a classical computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.2 defines the three categories.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper later places the quantum k-nearest neighbour algorithm in L2 (Section 2.6).

assertions.value: The authors state that in category L1 the overall process suffers no drawback from being computed entirely on a quantum machine, because classical computation can be performed efficiently on a quantum computer, and that protocols in this category have to consider limitations from read-in and read-out of the data.
quotes: the overall process suﬀers no drawback from being computed entirely on a quantum machine, as classical computation can be performed eﬃciently on a quantum computer [3, 10].
protocols within this category will have to carefully consider any limitations from read-in and read-out of the data on either side of the quantum computational process.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement, resting on cited references 3 and 10.

assertions.value: The authors state that, upon further inspection, much of the early work on quantum artificial neural networks seems to be quantum inspired: the algorithms can be described, understood and run efficiently on classical devices, but the inception of their idea stems from quantum concepts.

assertions.value: The authors state that the common approach of describing input vectors as quantum states and weights as operators, sometimes combined with measurement on each iteration to feed the output back classically, usually results in an algorithm that is incomplete (missing an appropriate training step, for example in references 16 and 35) or even disputed as incorrect (reference 37).

assertions.value: The authors report that Schuld et al. (reference 33), who propose quantum walks to build a quantum neural network with associative memory, prove that the naive case, where activation of a Hopfield network neuron is done using a biased coin, cannot work because the required neuron updating process is not unitary; a non-linearity is instead introduced through stochastic quantum walks on a hypercube.
quotes: Schuld et al. [33] propose using quantum walks to construct a quantum ANN algorithm,
However they prove that this cannot work as the required neuron updating process is not unitary.
Instead, a non-linearity is introduced through stochastic quantum walks (SQW) on a hypercube.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to reference 33; the paper does not reproduce the proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that Schuld et al. ran a few successful simulations illustrating the possibility of building an associative memory using stochastic quantum walks, with the walker ending up in the sink in a time dependent on the decoherent dynamics, and state that this is not a definitive answer to the artificial neural network problem since only some associative memory properties of the walk are demonstrated.
quotes: A few successful simulations were run, illustrating the possibility of building an associative memory using SQW, and showing that the walker ends up in the sink in a time dependent on the decoherent dynamics.
it is not a deﬁnitive answer to the ANN problem since Schuld et al. only demonstrate some associative memory properties of the walk.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a Boltzmann machine, classically computing the required gradient takes time exponential in the number of nodes of the network, so approximations are made such that the configuration can be efficiently calculated (reference 43).
quotes: Classically, computing the required gradient takes time exponential in the number of nodes of the network and so approximations are made such that the BM conﬁguration can be eﬃciently calculated [43].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to reference 43.

assertions.value: The authors report that Wiebe et al. (reference 44) developed two quantum algorithms that can efficiently calculate the Boltzmann machine configuration without approximations by efficiently preparing the Gibbs state; the second assumes access to the training data in superposition (through a QRAM), which reduces the complexity dependence quadratically on the number of training vectors.
quotes: Recently, Wiebe et al. have developed two quantum algorithms that can eﬃciently calculate the BM conﬁguration without approximations, by eﬃciently preparing the Gibbs state [44].
which reduces the complexity dependence quadratically on the number of training vectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to reference 44.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum deep learning does not provide a speedup over classical deep learning, so its advantage only comes from the accuracy of the solution, because in the asymptotic limit it converges to the exact solution while the classical algorithms can only converge to within a certain error; they add that Wiebe et al. acknowledge the algorithm is not efficient for all Boltzmann machine configurations, though it is conjectured that these problem machines will be rare.
quotes: QDL does not provide a speedup over CDL, and so the advantage only comes from the accuracy of the solution.
in the asymptotic limit, it converges to the exact solution.
The classical algorithms can only converge to within a certain error, depending on the approximation used.
Wiebe et al. acknowledge that their algorithm is not eﬃcient for all BM conﬁgurations, however it is conjectured that these problem BMs will be rare.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' summary of a cited algorithm; not derived in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 2.1.2 and the Appendix C table (quantum advantage lies in the solution being exact up to the error) agree that the claimed advantage is accuracy, not speed.

assertions.value: The authors state that an efficient classical equivalent of the quantum deep learning algorithm has been found (reference 45), and that this suggests quantum machine learning algorithms may lead to new classical algorithms, stressing the importance of this research even without a working quantum computer.
quotes: Recently, an eﬃcient classical equivalent of the QDL algorithm has been found [45].
QML algorithms may lead to new classical algorithms, stressing the importance of this research even without a working quantum computer.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum Bayesian networks and hidden quantum Markov models have been demonstrated theoretically in several papers, but that there is currently no experimental research (references 52, 53 and 54).

assertions.value: The authors state that any optimisation problem where the input is a data vector and the function to be optimised looks, at least locally, quadratic is really just solving a linear system of equations, so HHL may be considered a tool for solving generic optimisation problems in the same sense as classical methods like gradient descent or the conjugate gradient method.
quotes: Therefore, any optimisation problem where the input is a data vector and the function to be optimised over looks (at least locally) quadratic, is really just solving a linear system of equations.
HHL, then, may be considered a tool for solving generic optimisation problems in the same sense as classical methods like gradient descent or the conjugate gradient method.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short argument from Equations 5 and 6 in a review; the quadratic-functional step is stated, not proved as a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument takes the stationary point of a quadratic functional; it says nothing about the HHL caveats (sparsity, state input, state output), which the paper treats in Appendix A.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in contrast to other machine learning algorithms, the HHL algorithm is completely prescribed in the literature, strict lower bounds are known about its runtime and its caveats can be explicitly stated.

assertions.value: The authors report that Lloyd, Mohseni and Rebentrost's quantum PCA (reference 59) constructs the eigenvectors and eigenvalues in time O(Rlog(d)), where d and R are the dimensions of the spaces spanned by the density matrix and its principal-component approximation, and that for low-rank matrices this is an improvement over the classical algorithm that requires O(d) time.

in time O(Rlog(d)), where d and R are the dimensions of the space spanned by the

assertions.value: The authors state that for QPCA to gain a speedup some of the eigenvalues need to be large, and that for the case where all eigenvalues are equal and of size O(1/d) the algorithm reduces to scaling in time O(d), which offers no improvement over classical algorithms; they add that the necessity of QRAM and the scaling with the allowed error are further aspects, and that as of yet it is unclear how these requirements affect the applicability of the algorithm to real scenarios.

Other aspects that need to be considered include the necessity of QRAM and the scaling of the algorithm with the allowed error
As of yet, it is unclear how these requirements aﬀect the applicability of the algorithm to real scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors report that Lloyd et al. (reference 61) constructed a quantum nearest-centroid algorithm that only classifies vectors after the optimal clustering has been found, and that the same authors' quantum support vector machine (reference 62) rigorously confirmed the complexity arguments on the dependence on the vector length m.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum nearest-centroid algorithm has caveats: it only classifies data without performing the harder task of clustering, and it assumes access to a QRAM; they add that the potential of the adiabatic k-means algorithm in the same paper is hard to judge and is perhaps less promising due to the field's current focus on circuit-based architectures.
quotes: The algorithm has some caveats, in particular it only classiﬁes data without performing the harder task of clustering, and assumes access to a QRAM (see Section 4.3).

assertions.value: The authors report that clustering into k classes can be achieved by removing the k minus one longest connections of a minimum spanning tree, which takes Omega of N squared time classically (printed flat as N 2), and that Durr et al. show that if the connection matrix can be given by a quantum oracle the quantum computation time can be reduced using Grover's algorithm to Theta of N to the three halves (printed flat as N 3/2) (reference 68).

show that if the connection matrix of the minimum spanning tree can be given by a quantum oracle,

using algorithms as described by Du¨rr et al. for dimensionality reduction appears promising.

a quantum speedup is yet to be demonstrated [80].

assertions.value: The authors report that Cai et al. (reference 81) implemented a highly simplified version of Lloyd's supervised nearest-centroid algorithm on a small photonic quantum computer: a reference vector is chosen for each of two classes instead of clustering, all vectors are computed and stored classically before input to the quantum computer, two bismuth borate crystals create a four-qubit entangled state encoded in photon polarisations, and arbitrary 8-dimensional input and reference vectors can be encoded.

The implemented algorithm computes and stores all vectors classically before inputting them into the quantum computer.
using spontaneous parametric down-conversion to create a four-qubit entangled state encoded in the photon polarisations.
arbitrary 8-dimensional input and reference vectors can be encoded3.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the Cai et al. experiment the vectors are classified correctly the majority of the time, the classifier is prone to errors when the difference between the two distances is small, and the experimentally found distances typically differ from the true distances even after 500 measurements per vector (taking approximately 2 minutes); they state it is unclear whether this is an inherent problem with the algorithm or an artifact of the system, and that data is (selectively) provided in the paper.
quotes: In the paper, data is (selectively) provided, and the classiﬁer is demonstrated to be prone to errors when the diﬀerence between DA and DB is small.

Whilst the vectors are classiﬁed correctly the majority of the time, the experimentally found distances typically diﬀer from the true distances, even after 500 measurements per vector (taking approximately 2 minutes).
It is unclear whether this is an inherent problem with the algorithm or an artifact of the system it has been implemented on.

assertions.value: The authors report that Li et al. (reference 82) used a liquid-state nuclear magnetic resonance processor to run a quantum support vector machine on a simple pattern recognition problem of whether a hand-written number was a 6 or a 9, and that the experimental results show the machine was able to recognise the hand-written characters across all instances.
quotes: A recent attempt at implementing quantum machine learning using a liquid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) processor was carried out by Li et al. [82].
Their approach focused on solving a simple pattern recognition problem of whether a hand-written number was a 6 or a 9.
We can see that their machine was able to recognise the hand-written characters across all instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, reported second-hand.

assertions.value: The authors state that it has long been established that quantum entanglement is not present in any physical implementation of liquid-state NMR (references 84 and 85), and that as such it is highly likely that the work of Li et al. is only a classical simulation of quantum machine learning.
quotes: Unfortunately, it has long been established that quantum entanglement is not present in any physical implementation of liquid-state NMR [84, 85].
As such, it is highly likely that the work presented here is only a classical simulation of quantum machine learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' inference from cited results.

assertions.value: The authors state that HHL solves linear systems of equations exponentially faster than classical algorithms designed to tackle the same problem, and that it is therefore hoped that reformulating the support vector machine in a quantum environment will also result in a speedup.
quotes: HHL [55] solves linear systems of equations exponentially faster than classical algorithms designed to tackle the same problem.
Therefore, it is hoped that reformulating the support vector machine in a quantum environment will also result in a speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of a hope; the HHL speedup carries the caveats listed in Appendix A and is stated here without them.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponential statement is made without the sparsity, state-input and state-output conditions that Appendix A says HHL requires.

assertions.value: The authors state that a general purpose error-corrected quantum computer with a meaningful number of qubits is far from realisation, that it is not yet clear how many logical qubits are needed to outperform classical computers, and that no current qubit implementation solves all of the obstacles, which include coherence for the time of an algorithm, gates with approximately 0.1% error rates for error correction, and scalability.
assertions.anchor: 4.1 Practical Problems in Quantum Computing, p21
quotes: a general purpose errorcorrected quantum computer with a meaningful number of qubits is far from realisation.
It is not yet clear how many logical qubits quantum computers require to outperform classical computers
being able to implement gates with ≈0.1% error rates, such that quantum error correction may be performed [87],
No current qubit implementation solves all of these problems, though signiﬁcant progress continues to be made.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' 2015 assessment of hardware status, with the error-rate figure attributed to reference 87.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement dates from December 2015 and has not been checked against later hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is thought that quantum machine learning or quantum simulation may provide the first demonstration of a quantum speedup (references 11 and 86).
assertions.anchor: 4.1 Practical Problems in Quantum Computing, p21
quotes: it is thought that QML or quantum simulation may provide the ﬁrst demonstration of a quantum speedup [11, 86].
assertions.certainty_reason: A view the paper attributes to references 11 and 86.

assertions.value: The authors state that arbitrary state preparation is exponentially hard in the number of qubits for discrete gate sets (reference 3), providing a bound on the performance of all algorithms, and that a scheme claiming to encode data in the amplitudes of the exponentially large Hilbert space is questionable due to this exponential cost and readout issues.
quotes: Arbitrary state preparation is exponentially hard in the number of qubits for discrete gate sets [3], providing a bound on the performance of all algorithms
a scheme that claims to encode data using the amplitudes available in the exponentially large Hilbert space, is questionable due to this exponential cost
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to reference 3; the questioning of amplitude-encoding schemes is the authors' view.

assertions.value: The authors state that learning the pre-measurement state takes a number of trials exponential in system size, which kills any potential speedup, so any algorithm that outputs all the amplitudes of the final state suffers exponential costs, and that this argues against a useful quantum algorithm that stores output data in the exponentially large Hilbert space of a quantum state since the data would be impossible to retrieve.
quotes: Although it is possible to learn the pre-measurement state using a number of trials exponential in system size, this will kill any potential speedup.
This argues against the existence of a useful quantum algorithm that stores output data in the exponentially large Hilbert space of a quantum state - the data would be impossible to retrieve.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' argument, supported by a citation to Aaronson (reference 17) for what can be extracted.

assertions.value: The authors state that implementing a classical machine learning algorithm on a quantum device is simply using a quantum computer to do what a classical computer can achieve equally well and yields no quantum advantage, and that naive attempts to create a quantum machine learning algorithm by replacing all vectors in a classical algorithm with quantum states are usually unsuccessful at attaining a speed-up.
quotes: This is simply using a quantum computer to do what a classical computer can achieve equally well, and yields no quantum advantage.
attempts to create a QML algorithm by replacing all the vectors in a CML algorithm with quantum states, are usually unsuccessful at attaining a speed-up.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' general statement; not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the inclusion of QRAM in QML proposals is troubling from a theoretical and an experimental perspective, but that ruling out QRAM does not mean no datasets can be loaded efficiently: Grover and Rudolph (reference 93) discretise a function and sample it at 2n points (printed flat), which can be loaded into a superposition over n qubits efficiently provided there is an efficient classical algorithm to integrate the function over an arbitrary interval; whether meaningful datasets fall into this category is unclear.

assertions.value: The authors state that to date the majority of QML research has come from experts in either machine learning or quantum information and so oversights can be made, that the most successful advances have come from collaborations between classical machine learning and quantum information experts, and that early results highlight the promise of QML, where not only are time and space scalings possible but also more accurate classifiers.
quotes: To date, the majority of QML research has come from experts in either one of these two ﬁelds and, as such, oversights can be made.
The most successful advances in QML have come from collaborations between CML and quantum information experts, and this approach is highly encouraging.
These early results highlight the promise of QML, where not only are time and space scalings possible but also more accurate classiﬁers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusions from a literature review.

assertions.value: The authors state that QML research can help guide and advance classical machine learning and is important to pursue even though the hardware to implement useful instances of QML does not yet exist, and that there are several important issues to overcome before the practicality of QML becomes clear.
quotes: We would also like to stress that QML research can help guide and advance CML,
pursue even though we do not yet have the hardware to implement useful instances of QML.
There are several important issues to overcome before the practicality of QML becomes clear.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusions.

assertions.value: The authors state that considering what it means for a quantum system to learn could lead to novel quantum algorithms with no classical analogue.
quotes: Considering what it means for a quantum system to learn could lead to novel quantum algorithms with no classical analogue.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' speculation in the conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors state that Appendix A discusses a quantum algorithm that implements a perceptron, with a worst-case run-time asymptotically better than that which can be expected classically, and that this algorithm has been independently produced by the quantum engineering cohort.
quotes: The purpose of these notes is to discuss a quantum algorithm that implements a perceptron, with a worst-case run-time asymptotically better than that which can be expected classically.
This algorithm has been independently produced by the quantum engineering cohort.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix A opens by stating its own purpose and origin.

assertions.value: The authors define a perceptron as a supervised machine learning primitive where the goal is to produce a binary classifier that learns from a finite set of training data and then infers classifications for unlabelled data, and state that the appendix focuses on the simple perceptron example, since generalising opens up the field of neural networks, which is beyond their scope.
quotes: A perceptron is a supervised machine learning primitive where the goal is to produce a binary classiﬁer.
However, this generalisation opens up the ﬁeld of neural networks which is beyond our scope.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix A.1 defines the perceptron as the appendix uses it.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the earlier 'data in states' quantum perceptron approach the learning is still done classically, since measurement of the quantum state and a classical update rule are needed, and that it is difficult to see how a method requiring this level of classical read-out and updating could produce a speedup over a classical technique.
quotes: An issue with the method proposed is that the learning is still done classically.
It is diﬃcult to see how a method requiring this level of classical read-out and updating could produce a speedup over a classical technique.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' argument about earlier proposals.

assertions.value: The authors propose that the weights be encoded into the quantum state ('weights in states'), with the weights restricted for clarity to the value of 0 or 1, an operator encoding the training data acting on the initial weight state, and the extension to non-binary weights said to involve encoding the binary expansion of the weight in a string of qubits.
quotes: we instead propose that the weights wj be encoded into the state (hence ‘weights in states’).
the weights here can only take the value of 0 or 1, and so |w is a state vector in the computational basis.
the extension involves encoding the binary expansion of the weight in a string of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix A.2 states the setup of the proposed scheme.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for a correctly trained perceptron, finding weights that give the correct output for all training inputs is equivalent to solving the matrix equation Aw = y˜, which is exactly the kind of linear system solved by the HHL algorithm, so the operator in their circuit is given by the matrix A that must be inverted.
assertions.anchor: A.2 HHL Algorithm, p31-32, Equations 17 and 18
quotes: The equation Aw = y˜ is exactly the kind of linear system that is solved by the HHL algorithm.
Therefore, the operator Oˆ in Figure 16 is given by the matrix A that must be inverted in order to solve the linear system.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument in an appendix, with the matrix equation derived over Equations 17 and 18 but no theorem stated.
assertions.reader_inference: The reduction needs the training set to be exactly solvable, as the authors say in A.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that HHL has three technical caveats that loom largest: it requires the matrix A to be sparse, it takes a quantum state as input rather than a classical vector, and it outputs a quantum state rather than a classical vector.
quotes: We will address the three that loom largest: ﬁrstly, that HHL requires the matrix A be sparse; secondly, that it takes a quantum state as input, rather than a classical vector; and lastly, that it outputs a quantum state, rather than a classical vector.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' summary of caveats attributed to Aaronson (reference 17).

assertions.value: The authors state that the matrix A is constructed from training data that may or may not be sparse, depending on the problem and context, and that the only immediate remark is that the field of neural networks with sparse training data still covers a wide range of problems.
quotes: However, the matrix A is constructed from training data that may or may not be sparse, depending on the problem and context.
The only immediate remark is that the ﬁeld of neural networks with sparse training data still covers a wide range of problems
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix A states the sparsity condition is left unresolved for the perceptron.

assertions.value: The authors state that the input state for the perceptron application only requires preparing a computational basis state, because the training labels are drawn from the set containing 0 and 1 (and similarly the regularisers), so the circuit for this operation is of depth 1 and does not contribute to the complexity of the algorithm.
quotes: However, for this application, the quantities yt are just drawn from {0, 1} (and similarly for the regularisers bt), as the perceptron is a binary classiﬁer.
As such, the circuit for this operation is of depth 1 and does not contribute to the complexity of the algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument in an appendix; the authors state it without a numbered theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument treats the bias terms as binary too; the appendix does not discuss real-valued biases.

assertions.value: The authors state that HHL outputting a quantum state rather than a classical vector is not a valid concern for the perceptron: once the perceptron is trained and the weights fixed there is no interest in learning the values of the weights, and the weights can remain hidden in a state indefinitely while classifying new data.
assertions.anchor: A.2 Caveats to HHL, p32, Figure 17
quotes: However, this is not a valid concern here. Once the perceptron is trained, and the weights ﬁxed, there is no interest in learning the values of the weights.
the weights can remain hidden in a state indeﬁnitely without impacting on its ability to classify new data.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument in an appendix; the authors state it without a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument relies on the classification circuit consuming the trained weight state in place; the paper says that circuit is non-destructive on the weights.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as new data and weights are encoded in states in the computational basis, there is no reason why the classification scheme could not be performed equally well classically, although less naive classification schemes may differ markedly in the quantum and classical cases.
quotes: As new data and weights are encoded in states in the computational basis, there is no reason why this classiﬁcation scheme could not be performed equally well classically.
However, less na¨ıve classiﬁcation schemes may diﬀer markedly in the quantum and classical cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix A states this limit on its own classification stage.
assertions.reader_inference: By the paper's own L1/L2 definitions, this classification stage has a sub-routine that a classical computer performs equally well.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum speedup of their perceptron training algorithm is inherited from the quantum speedup of HHL, that the best possible classical iterative algorithm for this problem is the conjugate gradient method, that HHL offers an exponential improvement in N (the number of training instances) while scaling similarly in the error, and that provided the number of training instances N is much larger than the number of weights W they expect much better performance from the quantum algorithm.
assertions.anchor: A.2 Quantum Speedup, p33, Equations 19 to 22
quotes: The quantum speedup for this perceptron training algorithm is inherited from the quantum speedup of HHL.
where ε is a measure of error in the weight vector [56]. Conversely, the best possible classical iterative algorithm for this problem is the conjugate gradient method, which has a runtime of
HHL oﬀers an exponential improvement in N .
Therefore, provided that the number of training instances N is much larger than the number of weights, W , we can expect a much better performance from the quantum algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim, resting on complexity bounds for HHL and conjugate gradient taken from reference 56 and not derived in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The runtime expressions (Equations 19 to 22) were split across lines by the text layer and are not quoted; the claim of the best possible classical algorithm is stated without proof. The comparison also does not charge the cost of loading the training matrix, which Section 4.3 treats as the main problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is practically almost always the case that the number of training instances is much larger than the number of weights, and that exponentially more training instances than weights already gives an exponential speedup for the quantum algorithm, even for the naive classification scheme.
quotes: Practically, this is almost always the case.
In fact, exponentially more training instances than weights already gives an exponential speedup for the quantum algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim; no data on typical training-set sizes is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that their construction assumes that the weights of each feature can only take the value of 0 or 1, and that they have assumed there is a solution to the set of linear equations in Equation 18, meaning a combination of weights classifies all the training data correctly, which is often not the case, and it is unclear how the applicability of the algorithm will be affected.
quotes: The construction above assumes that the weights of each feature can only take the value of 0 or 1.
Speciﬁcally, we have assumed that there is a solution to the set of linear equations presented in Equation 18, i.e. there is a combination of weights that classiﬁes all the training data correctly.
This is often not the case and it is unclear how the applicability of the algorithm will be aﬀected.
assertions.certainty_reason: Appendix A.3 states the limits of its own construction.
assertions.reader_inference: The perceptron algorithm in A.2 therefore covers linearly separable (exactly solvable) training sets only, as the authors present it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the method can be generalised to non-binary weights by encoding a single weight in multiple qubits, producing an extra qubit overhead depending on the precision of the weights that should only contribute a logarithmic factor in precision to the total run time.
quotes: The method can be generalised to non-binary weights by encoding a single weight in multiple qubits.
but should only contribute a logarithmic factor in precision to the total run time of the algorithm.
